title: Advocating for view and daylight in buildings: Next steps
central_proposition: Addressing critical needs in research, simulation tools, and technology is essential to enable more effective use of daylight and view in buildings, thereby balancing human health and well-being with stringent energy efficiency and climate change mitigation goals.

concept_definitions.name: daylight
concept_definitions.definition: exposure to ambient levels of interior daylight illumination (and its associated spectral content)

concept_definitions.name: view
concept_definitions.definition: meaningful and desirable content of the ground plane, horizon, and/or sky outside and where details and movement of people, animals, landscape, and/or weather can be discerned.

concept_definitions.name: view clarity
concept_definitions.definition: the human eye's ability to perceive details of the outdoor environment without subjective interpretation of whether the content is interesting or of aesthetic value.

argument_structure: The paper first establishes the growing conflict between increasing urban density and urgent demands for building energy efficiency, while highlighting the increased awareness of daylight and view benefits for health and well-being. It then provides an overview of existing view-related research and metrics, followed by a discussion of current simulation models and their limitations. Finally, it identifies critical needs in research, tools, and technological advances to bridge the gap and enable integrated solutions that satisfy both human and environmental goals.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The paper synthesizes existing causal mechanisms, including intrinsically photoreceptive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) for circadian regulation, nature views for stress recovery and cognitive restoration (Biophilia, ART, SRT), and the influence of view content and clarity on psychological and physiological states (Prospect-Refuge). It also highlights how optical properties of glazing/shading, image resolution, and spectral composition affect visual perception and well-being. The core causal logic for future work is that integrated design and advanced technologies, guided by improved research and tools, can optimize the complex interplay between view, daylight, and energy performance to achieve holistic benefits.

findings.antecedent: Increased urban density and building energy efficiency demands
findings.consequent: Access to daylight and views; design options for daylight and views
findings.mechanism: Financial pressures on real estate development lead to taller, deeper floor-plate buildings and prescriptive constraints on window area in energy codes.
findings.quote: With the exponential growth in population and commensurate increased density in urban cities, access to daylight and views to nature is being severely curtailed in buildings.

findings.antecedent: View through a window (especially nature views)
findings.consequent: Recovery from surgery, mood, pain medication, post-surgical complications
findings.mechanism: Unspecified physiological and psychological benefits provided by natural light and views.
findings.quote: Ulrich found for example that gall bladder surgery patients with beds next to an outdoor view of nature (tree view)... recovered faster...

findings.antecedent: Brighter daylit wards in hospitals
findings.consequent: Average length of stay (ALOS) for patients
findings.mechanism: Likely physiological benefits provided by natural light.
findings.quote: It was found that patients in brighter daylit wards had a shorter ALOS.

findings.antecedent: Access to daylight and window views
findings.consequent: Myopia epidemic in children
findings.mechanism: Unspecified physiological benefits.
findings.quote: Greater access to daylight and window views has been advocated in school design to counter the growing myopia epidemic in children [23].

findings.antecedent: Intrinsically photoreceptive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) in the retina (most sensitive to 480 nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Signals to the circadian biological clock
findings.mechanism: ipRGCs detect specific wavelengths of light (blue sky, peak daylight intensity) and transmit signals that entrain the circadian rhythm.
findings.quote: intrinsically photoreceptive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) in the retina most sensitive to wavelengths at 480 nm... provide essential signals to our circadian biological clock [9-11].

findings.antecedent: Circadian biological clock signals
findings.consequent: Human physiology, health, and well-being (sleep patterns, alertness, memory formation, hunger, hormone release, blood pressure, body temperature, immune response)
findings.mechanism: Circadian rhythms regulate numerous bodily functions and processes.
findings.quote: These signals profoundly impact many aspects of human physiology, health, and well-being, including patterns of sleep, alertness, memory formation, hunger, hormone release, blood pressure, body temperature, and immune response.

findings.antecedent: Newly identified opsins in the eye (most sensitive to 380-430 nm violet light)
findings.consequent: Early eye development and other metabolic functions
findings.mechanism: Unspecified physiological role of these opsins.
findings.quote: newly identified opsins in the eye, most sensitive to violet light... may be involved in early eye development and other metabolic functions [15,16].

findings.antecedent: Working near a view window (office type tasks)
findings.consequent: Cognitive test performance, positive emotions, thermal comfort
findings.mechanism: Unspecified benefits of view access.
findings.quote: test subjects (n = 86) were found to perform better on cognitive tests, have more positive emotions and better thermal comfort after working on office type tasks near a view window...

findings.antecedent: Proportionally larger views (in office field studies)
findings.consequent: Performance
findings.mechanism: Unspecified benefits of view access.
findings.quote: Proportionally larger views were found to predict better performance in office field studies [48].

findings.antecedent: Access to "better" views (vegetation, sky, human activity outside)
findings.consequent: Positive outcomes in office and educational environments (greater working memory capacity, greater progress in math/reading, fewer health complaints, greater satisfaction with IEQ)
findings.mechanism: Multiple mechanisms at work, including circadian stimulus, cognitive and emotional mechanisms, along with social and cultural factors.
findings.quote: Access to "better" views... was consistently associated with a number of positive outcomes in office [49] and educational environments [50]...

findings.antecedent: View content (foreground and sky, close-up and far-away areas, visual complexity, natural materials/processes)
findings.consequent: View preferences, aesthetic pleasure, stress recovery
findings.mechanism: Contemplated evolutionary aesthetics (Dutton), prospect-refuge theory (Appleton), cognitive stimulus and relief from controlled indoor environments.
findings.quote: Prior research has focused on how human factors are affected by the specifics of view "content" and suggest that the best views include both foreground and sky...

findings.antecedent: Natural views and good view quality (aesthetic quality, composition, complexity)
findings.consequent: Psychological and physiological comfort, self-reported discomfort problems
findings.mechanism: Unspecified.
findings.quote: Researchers found that psychological and physiological comfort were positively influenced by natural views and good view quality.

findings.antecedent: View depth (distance from window to most distant visible element) and number of view layers
findings.consequent: Perceived view quality
findings.mechanism: Provides visual complexity and information, aligning with prospect-refuge theory.
findings.quote: The view depth... and number of view layers also had a strong positive influence on perceived view quality.

findings.antecedent: Glazing and shading materials (degree of obstruction, optical distortion, haze, scattering, spectral modification, reduction in dynamic range)
findings.consequent: Physiological and psychological benefits related to modified views
findings.mechanism: Modifies the visual information received by the eye, potentially impacting clarity, content, and spectral properties of the view.
findings.quote: Very little research has been conducted explicitly correlating physiological and psychological benefits to modified views as defined by degree of obstruction, optical distortion...
findings.empirical_support_cited: Very little research has been conducted explicitly correlating...

findings.antecedent: Shade materials (fabric openness factor, normal-hemispherical visible transmittance)
findings.consequent: View clarity
findings.mechanism: Optical properties of the material directly influence the ability to perceive details of the outdoor environment.
findings.quote: View clarity was found to be affected significantly by both sky conditions and viewing distance...

findings.antecedent: Automated access to unobstructed views with high lighting quality (compared to conventional offices with less reliable access and poor lighting)
findings.consequent: Occupant satisfaction, productive work environment
findings.mechanism: Combines benefits of view access with good lighting conditions, avoiding negative tradeoffs.
findings.quote: Results suggest that automated access to unobstructed views with high lighting quality can create a more satisfactory, productive work environment...

findings.antecedent: Occupants' choice of EC window over venetian blind (to satisfy visual constraints)
findings.consequent: Satisfaction with workplace environment
findings.mechanism: EC windows provide better view access and less glare compared to venetian blinds, leading to improved comfort and preference.
findings.quote: 85% of occupants preferred the EC windows over the reference windows, with more view and less glare being contributing factors for the preference.

findings.antecedent: View through a shade (fabric, venetian blinds, frosted glass, electrochromic glazing)
findings.consequent: Perception of view (affected by outdoor daylight conditions, direct/diffuse scattering)
findings.mechanism: The optical properties of the shade interact with incident radiation, and the human visual system processes the resulting light, affecting clarity and detail perception.
findings.quote: Is view through a shade... a pure material or system property... Or do outdoor daylight conditions contribute significantly to the perception of the view...
findings.empirical_support_cited: important questions that remain when trying to evaluate view within the daylighting design aspects...

findings.antecedent: Degradation in view image quality (due to imbalance between direct and scattered radiation, haze, glare from minute openings)
findings.consequent: Obscured view
findings.mechanism: Scattered light reduces contrast and detail perception, making it harder to discern objects.
findings.quote: Degradation in view image quality occurs due to an imbalance between direct and scattered radiation.

findings.antecedent: High-resolution, photorealistic, physically based images (for simulation)
findings.consequent: Clarity of distant rendered objects
findings.mechanism: Image resolution inherently limits the amount of detail that can be represented, affecting the ability to discern small or distant features.
findings.quote: Image resolution... limits the degree of clarity of distant rendered objects (Fig. 3).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Image resolution... limits the degree of clarity of distant rendered objects (Fig. 3).

findings.antecedent: Spectral composition of transmitted daylight and solar radiation (modified by window glass/shading)
findings.consequent: Color rendering of outdoor objects, naturalness of view
findings.mechanism: Spectral properties determine the color of light reaching the eye, influencing how colors are perceived and the overall naturalness of the scene.
findings.quote: The naturalness of the view is affected by the spectral composition [90] of transmitted daylight.

findings.antecedent: Spatial frequency of the stimulus (e.g., shading materials creating patterns)
findings.consequent: Visual perception, visual discomfort (e.g., moire effect)
findings.mechanism: The eye's neural sensitivity to specific spatial frequencies can lead to discomfort if patterns interfere with visual processing.
findings.quote: The eye's neural sensitivity to spatial frequency of the stimulus affects visual perception [97,98].

findings.antecedent: Veiling reflections (produced by interior reflections off indoor glass surface)
findings.consequent: Obscured views
findings.mechanism: Reflections reduce contrast and clarity of the view through the window.
findings.quote: Views can also be obscured by veiling reflections produced by interior reflections of white or bright objects off the indoor glass surface of the window.

findings.antecedent: Integrated analysis (of view, daylight, thermal comfort, energy use, etc.)
findings.consequent: Satisfaction of health/well-being and energy efficiency requirements
findings.mechanism: Multi-objective optimization and parametric analysis allow designers to identify optimal solutions that balance competing demands.
findings.quote: Integrated analysis is ideal if the goal is to satisfy health and well-being as well as stringent building energy efficiency requirements.

findings.antecedent: Thermal performance of windows (U-factors reduced to 0.6 W/m²-K or lower)
findings.consequent: Heating impacts of windows, ability to increase window area for views
findings.mechanism: Highly insulating glazings reduce heat loss, making larger windows feasible without significant energy penalty.
findings.quote: With these levels of thermal performance, the heating impacts of windows... can be minimized in even the coldest climates, allowing some increase in window area if needed to provide views without incurring a significant energy or comfort penalty.

findings.antecedent: Spectrally selective, low-emittance coatings (rejecting solar near-infrared energy with modest daylight loss)
findings.consequent: Solar impacts on cooling, visible light transmission, view
findings.mechanism: Coatings selectively filter wavelengths, allowing visible light through while blocking heat-generating infrared radiation.
findings.quote: coatings can reject virtually all of the solar near-infrared energy with only a modest loss of daylight using complex multilayer coatings...

findings.antecedent: Spectrally selective glazings (reducing transmittance in 300-400 nm range)
findings.consequent: Melanopic and violet light exposures for physiological requirements
findings.mechanism: Filtering specific wavelengths impacts the non-visual photoreceptors involved in circadian regulation and other physiological processes.
findings.quote: Since the spectral content of transmitted daylight affects melanopic and violet light exposures for physiological requirements, this aspect of spectral selectivity should be further investigated.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Since the spectral content of transmitted daylight affects melanopic and violet light exposures for physiological requirements, this aspect of spectral selectivity should be further investigated.

findings.antecedent: Smart switchable glass (electrochromic, variable tint zones, neutral gray appearance)
findings.consequent: Visible transmittance, solar heat gains, energy and glare management, transparent view
findings.mechanism: Electrical control changes the optical properties of the glass, allowing dynamic adjustment of light and heat transmission.
findings.quote: The latest generation of switchable transparent electrochromic (EC) glass modulates visible transmittance and solar heat gains over a wide dynamic range...

findings.antecedent: Optically complex shading systems (geometrically complex slats, multilayer fabrics, honeycomb structures, electrochromic threads, shape memory alloys)
findings.consequent: Management of incident sunlight, transparency, view
findings.mechanism: Advanced materials and designs allow dynamic control over optical properties and geometry, adapting to solar conditions and user needs.
findings.quote: Blinds and louver systems have evolved from simple slatted assemblies to geometrically complex slats... Shades have evolved from single layer fabrics to more complex multilayer, honeycomb structures...

findings.antecedent: Luminance contrast within spatial frequencies (where humans are most sensitive)
findings.consequent: Visual comfort
findings.mechanism: High contrast at sensitive spatial frequencies can cause visual discomfort and interfere with visual processing.
findings.quote: Avoiding luminance contrast within spatial frequencies where we are most sensitive will ensure visual comfort (Fig. 6).

findings.antecedent: Patterns inspired by nature (in shading systems)
findings.consequent: Calming, interesting, pleasant feelings, stress recovery
findings.mechanism: Biophilic response to natural patterns.
findings.quote: Patterns inspired by nature were evaluated as calming, interesting and pleasant, which raises the question on how such elements could be applied in design to support stress recovery (Fig. 6) [128,129].

findings.antecedent: Overhangs, awnings, fixed horizontal louver systems, screens
findings.consequent: Views of the sky
findings.mechanism: Physical obstruction.
findings.quote: Many shading systems such as overhangs, awnings, and fixed horizontal louver systems or screens block views of the sky.

findings.antecedent: Separation of view from daylight apertures (e.g., separate windows for view and daylight, or specific shading strategies)
findings.consequent: Access to view, need for larger-area windows, balanced daylight/view/energy use
findings.mechanism: Allows independent control of view and daylight, optimizing each function without compromising the other.
findings.quote: Separation of view from daylight apertures enable control of shades for independent purposes [136-138] (Fig. 8).

findings.antecedent: Light shelf or prismatic glazing in clerestory portion of window
findings.consequent: Daylight redirection to ceiling deeper into room, energy use, circadian health, views of the sky
findings.mechanism: Optical properties redirect light, but physical presence obstructs direct views.
findings.quote: a light shelf or prismatic glazing in the clerestory portion of the window will redirect daylight to the ceiling deeper into a room... but will block or obscure views of the sky [139].

findings.antecedent: Skylight or light pipe (collecting sunlight at exterior/roof, transporting to core/below-ground)
findings.consequent: Circadian entrainment, reduced energy, resiliency, visual clues to outdoor conditions, access to windows/views
findings.mechanism: Transports natural light to areas without direct window access, providing both visual and non-visual benefits.
findings.quote: A skylight or light pipe collects sunlight at the exterior wall or roof and transports daylight and/or sunlight to the core or below-ground spaces that have no access to windows or views.

findings.antecedent: Building integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) as window glazing (traditional silicon cells, amorphous silicon)
findings.consequent: Color and clarity of view out of windows
findings.mechanism: The materials used in BIPV can alter the optical properties of the window, affecting how light is transmitted and colors are perceived.
findings.quote: When used as window glazing, the current commercial technologies... have a significant impact on the color and clarity of view out of windows.

findings.antecedent: "Clear" PV windows (converting solar near infrared/UV to electricity, maintaining transparent view with minimal visible transmittance impact)
findings.consequent: Power generation, view
findings.mechanism: Specialized PV materials allow visible light to pass through while converting non-visible solar radiation into electricity.
findings.quote: Several startups making good progress on PV windows that convert solar near infrared and ultraviolet light to electricity and maintain a transparent view with minimal impacts on visible transmittance [141].

findings.antecedent: Smart sensors and building controls (sensing occupancy, thermal conditions, utility rates, building energy use history, occupant preferences)
findings.consequent: Optimization of operable glazing and shading systems (for occupant view, building carbon emissions)
findings.mechanism: Data-driven, adaptive control algorithms can dynamically adjust window systems to balance multiple performance objectives.
findings.quote: A new generation of smart sensors and building controls... can now, in principle, evaluate and optimize control of operable glazing and shading systems...

findings.antecedent: Real estate market (speculative developments, maximizing narrowly defined return-on-investments)
findings.consequent: Use of advanced technologies, advocacy for health/well-being in buildings, occupant-friendly indoor environments
findings.mechanism: Economic incentives and market pressures dictate the adoption of new technologies and design approaches.
findings.quote: the reality is that speculative developments based on maximizing narrowly defined return-on-investments will likely continue to drive the mainstream real estate market...

findings.antecedent: Clear research evidence, accurate/efficient tools for practitioners, turnkey/intelligent technological solutions
findings.consequent: Economic rationale for investments in window views/occupant satisfaction/building performance
findings.mechanism: Providing robust data and practical solutions reduces risk and increases perceived value for real estate developers.
findings.quote: A better understanding of the relationship between window views, occupant satisfaction and building performance will help strengthen the economic rationale for these investments.

findings.antecedent: Users' interaction with building systems (lighting, shading)
findings.consequent: Occurs only at beginning of day or during prolonged discomfort
findings.mechanism: Habituation and adaptation to environmental conditions, or lack of effective control options.
findings.quote: Field studies show that users interact with building systems (lighting, shading, etc.) only at the beginning of the day or in the case of prolonged discomfort [145,146].

findings.antecedent: Individual's access to view (especially in landscape office)
findings.consequent: Ability to fix if uncomfortable
findings.mechanism: Lack of personal control or effective solutions in open-plan environments.
findings.quote: But an individual's access to the view can be difficult to fix, especially in a landscape office.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: There is a minimum threshold and/or optimal range of greenery percentage/quality in a view that maximizes stress recovery and cognitive restoration.
Specific qualities of greenery (texture, lushness, formalism, color composition) beyond mere quantity modulate the restorative effect of nature views.
A minimum angular size of view, or view area, is required to elicit health and well-being benefits.
There are specific temporal and spatial obstruction thresholds for shading devices beyond which the health and well-being benefits of a window view are significantly diminished.
Specific temporal patterns (timing, duration) and intensity of sunlight exposure are required to elicit positive psychological effects (e.g., mood, emotions).
The perception of view through a shade is significantly influenced by dynamic outdoor daylight conditions (direct/diffuse scattering) and not solely by the static optical properties of the material.
A specific level of geometric detail in simulations is necessary to accurately predict human perception of view clarity through complex shading systems.
Neurocognitive models can accurately translate simulated visual input into perceived mental images, and these mental images can be correlated with stress-reducing and restorative effects.
Current BSDF methods are insufficient for accurately modeling view clarity through spatially inhomogeneous shading systems, requiring new methods.
Spectral simulations are necessary to accurately evaluate the impact of color on perceived views, especially with spectrally selective materials.
bridge_warrants: The paper integrates concepts from Biophilia, Stress Recovery Theory (SRT), and Attention Restoration Theory (ART) to explain the health and well-being benefits of nature views.
It connects circadian regulation (CB) to light exposure and view characteristics, emphasizing the role of non-visual photoreception.
The paper links cognitive performance (T20) and emotional states (NM, IC) to view access and quality, highlighting the need for integrated design.
It discusses how economic factors and market dynamics (T_IE_003) influence the adoption of advanced building technologies that impact view and daylight.
methodological_critiques: Lack of knowledge regarding the complex causal mechanisms of window views on human factors is a severely limiting factor in forward progress.
Current models and methods to derive bidirectional scattering distribution functions (BSDFs) will need to be modified.
Very little is known about daylight exposure patterns for various population types.

Very little research has been conducted explicitly correlating physiological and psychological benefits to modified views as defined by degree of obstruction, optical distortion, haze, scattering, spectral modification, and reduction in the dynamic range of light intensity by glazing and shading materials.
Given known limitations of VR [65], further studies under real world conditions are planned to support hypotheses to date.
Documentation of window and shading conditions affecting view clarity is often missing or of insufficient detail in real-world studies.
Including all aspects of view clarity in run-time simulations is likely not feasible and/or computationally efficient with today's tools and available optical data.
Achieving spectral accuracy in renderings will require model and input data updates, particularly if view clarity is based on visual perception metrics (e.g., contrast and complexity).
Control models for manually operated shading systems are limited and represent a serious limitation in the evaluation of view in buildings with conventional shades.
model_structure: The paper proposes a framework for integrated analysis and design, emphasizing a multi-objective approach that considers view access, content, and clarity alongside energy performance. It advocates for a holistic design process that leverages advanced technologies and simulation tools to balance human health and well-being with environmental goals.
limitations: Lack of knowledge regarding the complex causal mechanisms of window views on human factors.
Current models and methods to derive bidirectional scattering distribution functions (BSDFs) need modification.
Very little is known about daylight exposure patterns for various population types.
The underlying causal mechanisms of view benefits are less well understood.
Very little research has explicitly correlated physiological/psychological benefits to modified views by glazing/shading materials.
Limitations of virtual reality (VR) for view perception studies.
Documentation of window and shading conditions affecting view clarity is often missing or insufficient in real-world studies.
Ambiguous correlations between office type/location and occupant satisfaction.
Unclear if current image resolution is sufficient to discern fine details in distant objects.
Higher resolved spectral calculations may be needed for spectrally selective materials.
Replicating stereoscopic vision for depth perception is a challenge.
Including all aspects of view clarity in run-time simulations is not currently feasible or computationally efficient.
Even the smartest automated systems may not meet all occupant needs, requiring manual overrides.
The importance of views of the sky versus horizontal/downward views is not fully known.
The relative value of daylight-redirecting technologies and view needs to be better understood.
Current BIPV technologies can significantly impact view color and clarity.
Occupant desire for view and response to views is not uniform or constant over time.
Users typically interact with building systems only at the beginning of the day or during prolonged discomfort.
An individual's access to view can be difficult to fix, especially in open-plan offices.
